title: Why Not Just Use One Big Database for Everything?
summary: Tests whether you can justify decomposing storage — sharding, polyglot persistence, service boundaries — against the honest simplicity of a single database, instead of assuming decomposition is always correct.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"why not just use one big database for everything?"** This is a legitimate challenge, not a naive question to brush aside — a single database really does handle most systems fine, and the burden of proof is on decomposing it, not the other way around.

A strong answer defaults to one database and justifies any split with a specific, named limit — never a generic belief that "one database doesn't scale."

Ask what's actually driving the move away from one database: is it write throughput a single instance can't sustain, a data shape (graph, full-text, time-series) the relational model handles poorly, or organizational boundaries between teams?

Each of these three points to a different fix — sharding for write throughput, polyglot persistence for data shape, and separate services for organizational boundaries. Answering before identifying which one applies here produces a generic, unconvincing justification.

Start from one database as the default. Only decompose when a specific, named limit of a single instance is actually being hit — not preemptively, and not because decomposition is assumed to be the mature choice.

The burden of proof works in one direction: you need a concrete reason to split, you don't need a reason to stay simple. "We might need it later" is not a specific, named limit.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: how far one database actually goes
slides.markdown:
A single well-tuned Postgres instance can comfortably handle tens of thousands of QPS and terabytes of data for most applications. The decision to shard or split databases should point at the specific number this system will exceed, not a generic belief that "one database doesn't scale."

Many interview candidates jump to sharding for systems whose actual projected load is a fraction of what one good instance already handles — naming the real ceiling first prevents that.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a genuine data-shape gap
slides.markdown:
A social app's single Postgres instance is fine for the relational core — users, posts, follows. But full-text search across posts is slow and awkward in SQL at scale. Adding [polyglot-persistence](polyglot-persistence) — Elasticsearch *just* for search — is justified by a specific, named gap, not a wholesale abandonment of the single database.

The relational core stays exactly as it was; only the piece with a genuine data-shape mismatch gets its own store. This is a narrow, targeted decomposition, not a general philosophy of "split everything."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the organizational case for decomposition
slides.markdown:
![Separate databases per team versus one shared database](assets/separate-vs-shared-db.svg)

A distinct case from technical load: two teams that both need to evolve their own schema independently, and deploy on their own schedule, may justify separate databases even before either team's technical load requires it — because shared-database coupling is itself the bottleneck.

This is an organizational limit, not a technical one, and it's just as valid a specific, named reason as a throughput ceiling.

assets.alt: Separate databases per team versus one shared database

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
| | One database | Split databases |
|---|---|---|
| Transactions & joins | Free, built-in | Lost — replaced by sagas or application-level joins |
| Mental model | Single, simple | Multiple stores, multiple failure modes |
| Scaling | Vertical, then a real ceiling | Independent per store, independent team ownership |

**How to decide:** splitting doesn't remove complexity, it relocates it — from the database into your application and operational layers — so only pay that price once a specific, named limit of the single database is actually hit.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you join across three databases now?
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "you've split into three databases — how do you now do a query that used to be a simple join across them?" Either denormalize or duplicate the needed data into each service ahead of time, or accept a slower application-level join — fetch from each store and merge in code.

Both are real costs the single database didn't have. Naming this cost explicitly, rather than glossing over it, is part of what makes the decomposition decision credible.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: when does one big database actually become wrong?
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "at what point does 'one big database' actually become the wrong call?" When you can point to a specific, measured limit — a write-throughput ceiling, a genuine data-shape mismatch, or a real team-autonomy bottleneck — rather than a general anxiety about scale.

The answer is deliberately the same shape as the answer skeleton: name the concrete limit. If you can't name one, the single database is still the right call.

**Wrong belief:** decomposing into multiple databases preemptively "for scale" before any specific limit of a single database has actually been identified.

**Why it's wrong:** this pays the full complexity cost — lost transactions, a translation layer for cross-store joins, more operational surface area — with none of the benefit yet earned, since the load that would have justified the split hasn't arrived.

**Correct model:** stay on one database until a specific, named limit is measured, then decompose to address exactly that limit.

Default to one database — a single well-tuned instance goes further than most candidates assume. Split only when you can name a specific limit: write throughput, a data-shape mismatch handled better by another store, or a real organizational bottleneck between teams.

When you do split, name the cost honestly — lost transactions and joins, replaced by sagas or application-level merges — since splitting relocates complexity rather than removing it. Compare this to [sql-vs-nosql-at-scale](sql-vs-nosql-at-scale) for the data-shape side of this decision in more depth.
